lines.text: Understanding car parts and basic mechanics empowers drivers to communicate confidently with garages, make informed decisions about repairs, and handle minor roadside emergencies. Under the bonnet (hood in American English), the engine is the heart of the vehicle. Modern petrol and diesel engines are internal combustion engines — fuel is ignited inside cylinders, driving pistons that turn the crankshaft. The battery provides electrical power for starting the engine and running accessories. The radiator cools the engine by circulating coolant (a water-antifreeze mixture) through the engine block. The alternator recharges the battery while the engine is running. Beneath the car, the exhaust system channels waste gases from the engine through the catalytic converter (which reduces harmful emissions) and out through the tailpipe. The braking system uses hydraulic fluid to press brake pads against discs (or drums on older cars), converting motion into heat through friction. Tyres are the only contact point between the car and the road — their tread depth, pressure, and condition are critical safety factors. The legal minimum tread depth in the UK is 1.6 millimetres. The suspension system — springs, shock absorbers, and anti-roll bars — absorbs road imperfections and keeps the tyres in contact with the surface. The gearbox (transmission) transfers engine power to the wheels, with manual gearboxes requiring the driver to change gear using a clutch pedal and gear stick.
